subtopic_detail: Painful vulval and vaginal erosions with scarring in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 61 year old woman attends your clinic with 14 months of vulval soreness and burning that is worse on urination and makes intercourse impossible. She has tried two courses of antifungal cream and a barrier ointment without benefit.

She also reports painful gums that bleed when brushing and a rough patch inside her cheek. On examination there is loss of the labia minora with early adhesion of the introitus, and glazed red erosions with a fine white lacy border at the introitus and lower vagina. The clitoral hood is not fused and there are no white parchment-like plaques on the perineum or perianal skin. A vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogens.

data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions at the introitus and lower vagina with a reticulate white border; loss of labia minora; buccal mucosa shows a white lacy pattern; no perianal involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an extended course of oral fluconazole for resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.rationale: Two antifungal courses have failed and swabs show no candida, so continuing this line ignores the negative result and the mucosal findings elsewhere. Extended fluconazole is appropriate for microbiologically confirmed recurrent candidiasis. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review the symptoms after three months
options.rationale: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes pallor, dryness and thinning rather than glazed erosions with a lacy white border, and it does not affect the mouth. Vaginal oestrogen is a useful adjunct here but will not control the underlying inflammatory disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the introital adhesions before any medical treatment starts
options.rationale: Operating on actively inflamed mucosa leads to recurrent scarring and poor healing, so inflammation must be controlled first. Surgery has a limited role later for persistent adhesions once the disease is quiescent. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)

options.text: Prescribe an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid and arrange biopsy with long term review
options.rationale: Erosive mucosal disease with a reticulate white border affecting both the vulva and the mouth requires an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid as first line therapy, with biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy given the long duration. Lifelong surveillance is needed because of a recognised risk of squamous cell carcinoma in affected skin. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Skin Disorders)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

options.text: Prescribe topical lidocaine gel and refer to a pelvic pain service for vulvodynia management
options.rationale: Vulvodynia is defined by pain without visible pathology, and she has clear erosions, scarring and mucosal disease, so a pain-only pathway would leave destructive inflammation untreated. Topical anaesthetic is a symptomatic adjunct at best. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen planus and lichen sclerosus are the two inflammatory dermatoses that scar the vulva, and separating them matters because the erosive form of lichen planus involves the vagina and other mucosal surfaces while lichen sclerosus does not. Lichen sclerosus produces white parchment-like plaques in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus with clitoral hood fusion, whereas erosive lichen planus produces glazed red erosions with a reticulate white border at the introitus and in the vagina, often with oral involvement and gingivitis. Vaginal involvement is important because adhesions can obliterate the vagina entirely if untreated. Both conditions are treated first line with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, usually as a reducing regimen, and both carry a small but definite risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma that mandates ongoing review. Biopsy is indicated where the diagnosis is uncertain, where disease fails to respond to adequate treatment, or where a lesion looks suspicious.
key_points: Erosive lichen planus involves the vagina and mouth; lichen sclerosus spares both
A reticulate white border around glazed erosions is the characteristic sign
Lichen sclerosus shows a figure of eight distribution with perianal involvement and hood fusion
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line for both conditions
Both carry a risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma requiring long term surveillance
explanation.pearls: Vaginal involvement is what makes erosive lichen planus dangerous: untreated adhesions can obliterate the vagina, so vaginal dilators and topical corticosteroid are used alongside vulval treatment rather than after it.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Vulval Lichen Planus

subtopic_detail: Interpreting an abnormal thyroid stimulating hormone in early pregnancy
stem:
You review a 32 year old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy who had thyroid function tested by her general practitioner because of fatigue. She has no goitre, no cold intolerance, no constipation and no dry skin, and her weight is stable.

She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease and has never had neck irradiation. She takes a pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine. On examination her pulse is regular, there is no tremor, no lid lag and no palpable thyroid enlargement. She is anxious about the result and asks whether her baby will be affected.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 5.8 mIU/L (pregnancy specific upper limit for the first trimester 4.0), free thyroxine 13.1 pmol/L (10.0-20.0), thyroid peroxidase antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence levothyroxine now and repeat thyroid function testing in four weeks
options.rationale: A thyroid stimulating hormone above the pregnancy specific reference limit with a normal free thyroxine and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies is the combination in which treatment is recommended, because antibody positivity predicts progression to overt hypothyroidism as gestational demand rises. Repeat testing at four weeks allows titration during the period of greatest foetal dependence. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function test in the second trimester without commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Deferring treatment wastes the first trimester, during which the foetus depends entirely on maternal thyroxine for neurodevelopment, and antibody positivity makes deterioration likely rather than possible. Watchful waiting is reasonable only when antibodies are negative and the elevation is marginal. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her that the result is normal for pregnancy and requires no further action
options.rationale: This misreads the reference interval, since the pregnancy specific upper limit is lower than the non-pregnant one because human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates the thyroid and suppresses the pituitary hormone. A value of 5.8 mIU/L is therefore clearly abnormal in the first trimester. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake scanning to define the underlying cause
options.rationale: Radionuclide scanning is contraindicated in pregnancy and ultrasound does not alter management when the antibody result already indicates autoimmune thyroiditis. Imaging is indicated for a palpable nodule or goitre. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Increase her dietary iodine intake and recheck thyroid function after eight weeks
options.rationale: She already takes an iodine containing supplement, and iodine repletion does not correct autoimmune thyroid failure. Dietary iodine advice addresses deficiency in populations with inadequate intake rather than antibody mediated disease. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Thyroid physiology changes substantially in pregnancy, with human chorionic gonadotropin weakly stimulating the thyroid receptor and thereby suppressing the pituitary hormone, so pregnancy specific reference intervals are lower than non-pregnant ones and applying the wrong interval is a frequent source of error. Subclinical hypothyroidism means an elevated thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine, and the decision to treat rests substantially on thyroid peroxidase antibody status, since antibody positive women are far more likely to progress to overt hypothyroidism as gestational demand increases. Foetal thyroid hormone production does not begin until around 12 weeks, so the developing brain depends entirely on maternal supply through the first trimester, which is why treatment is started promptly rather than deferred. Women already on levothyroxine before conception typically require a dose increase of 25 to 30 per cent as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Antibody positive women also carry an increased risk of postpartum thyroiditis and need thyroid function checked after delivery.
key_points: Pregnancy specific reference intervals are lower; using non-pregnant ranges causes missed diagnoses
Thyroid peroxidase antibody status drives the treatment decision in subclinical hypothyroidism
The foetal thyroid does not function until around 12 weeks, so early maternal supply is critical
Radionuclide scanning is contraindicated during pregnancy
Antibody positive women require postpartum thyroid function testing
explanation.pearls: A woman already taking levothyroxine needs roughly a 25 to 30 per cent dose increase from the moment pregnancy is confirmed, most simply achieved by taking two extra tablets per week while awaiting formal review.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Antiseizure medication review in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 27 year old woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures attends your clinic to discuss becoming pregnant in the next year. She has been seizure free for four years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having previously failed a trial of levetiracetam because of intolerable irritability.

She drives to work and describes her independence as very important to her. She takes no other medicines and does not smoke or drink. She has read online that her medicine is dangerous in pregnancy and has already stopped taking it three days ago without telling anyone. She has had no seizures since stopping and feels well.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, ceased three days ago by the patient; no folate supplement; no other regular medicines

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Advise her to restart her medicine today and arrange urgent neurology review for a planned switch
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal risks breakthrough seizures and status epilepticus, which carry greater immediate danger to her than the teratogenic risk of a medicine taken before conception, so restarting while a supervised change is organised is the safest step. A cross-taper to a lower risk agent is then planned with contraception maintained until she is stable. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy)

options.text: Support her decision to remain off treatment given four years of seizure freedom
options.rationale: Seizure freedom on treatment is not evidence that treatment can be stopped, and withdrawal after four years still carries a substantial relapse rate that is highest in the first months. Planned withdrawal is a specialist decision made with driving and safety implications discussed in advance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence high dose folic acid and advise her to conceive as soon as possible while off treatment
options.rationale: Folate is important but does not protect against seizures, and encouraging conception during an unsupervised medication gap places both her and a pregnancy at risk. Folate should be started once a stable regimen is in place. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy)

options.text: Substitute levetiracetam at full dose today given her plan to conceive within the year
options.rationale: An abrupt switch without cross-tapering risks breakthrough seizures, and she has already failed this agent for behavioural side effects, making it a poor choice without specialist reassessment. Any change requires overlapping titration under supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange serum valproate concentration measurement before deciding on any change to therapy
options.rationale: Drug levels do not guide management here because she has already stopped the medicine and the decision rests on seizure risk rather than concentration. Levels are more useful for assessing adherence or toxicity during ongoing therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiseizure medicines, with major congenital malformation rates around 10 per cent and a substantial risk of impaired neurodevelopment in exposed children, which is why regulatory authorities require that it not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other options have failed and pregnancy prevention is in place. The clinical dilemma arises when a woman is well controlled on it, because abrupt cessation is genuinely dangerous and uncontrolled generalised seizures in pregnancy risk maternal injury, foetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The correct approach is never to stop abruptly but to restart, then cross-taper to a lower risk agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam under specialist supervision, with effective contraception maintained throughout the change and until control is confirmed. High dose folic acid is recommended before conception for women taking antiseizure medicines. Pregnancy itself alters drug handling, and lamotrigine concentrations in particular fall substantially, requiring dose increases and postpartum reduction.
key_points: Never stop an antiseizure medicine abruptly; withdrawal seizures are the immediate danger
Valproate carries roughly a 10 per cent malformation rate plus neurodevelopmental risk
Changing agents requires a supervised cross-taper with contraception maintained throughout
High dose folic acid is recommended preconception for women on antiseizure medicines
Uncontrolled generalised seizures in pregnancy risk maternal injury and foetal hypoxia
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine concentrations can fall by more than half during pregnancy through increased glucuronidation, so levels need monitoring with dose increases through gestation and a prompt reduction in the first weeks after birth to avoid toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Perineal assessment immediately after an assisted vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar who has just performed a forceps birth for a prolonged second stage in a 31 year old woman in her first pregnancy. The baby weighed 4.1 kg and a mediolateral episiotomy was performed. Blood loss is 350 mL and the uterus is well contracted.

You are inspecting the perineum before repair with adequate regional analgesia and good lighting. The episiotomy extends towards the anal margin. On systematic examination with a lubricated gloved finger in the rectum and a thumb in the vagina, you can feel a defect in the external anal sphincter involving approximately half its thickness, with the internal sphincter appearing intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy extending to the anal margin; partial thickness external anal sphincter defect; internal anal sphincter intact; anal mucosa intact

lead_in: How should this injury be classified and managed?

options.text: Second degree tear, repaired in the birth room using a continuous absorbable suture technique
options.rationale: A second degree tear involves perineal muscle without any sphincter involvement, and a sphincter defect has been identified, so this classification would lead to inadequate repair. Birth room repair without sphincter reconstruction is appropriate only when the sphincter is confirmed intact. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Third degree tear subcategory a, repaired in the birth room with a standard perineal technique
options.rationale: The subcategory is wrong because a defect involving half the sphincter thickness exceeds the threshold that defines subcategory a, and the location of repair is also wrong since sphincter injury requires theatre. Subcategory a describes a defect of less than half the external sphincter thickness. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Fourth degree tear, repaired in theatre with anal mucosal repair before sphincter reconstruction
options.rationale: A fourth degree tear requires breach of the anal epithelium, and the mucosa is explicitly intact here, so this overstates the injury. The distinction matters because mucosal repair and its antibiotic and follow up implications differ. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Third degree tear subcategory b, repaired in theatre by an appropriately trained operator
options.rationale: A defect involving more than half the external sphincter thickness with an intact internal sphincter and intact anal mucosa defines subcategory b, and every sphincter injury is repaired in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia, good lighting and an experienced operator. Adequate anaesthesia allows the retracted sphincter ends to be retrieved and approximated properly. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Third degree tear subcategory c, managed conservatively with a delayed secondary repair at three months
options.rationale: Subcategory c denotes internal sphincter involvement, which is absent here, and delaying repair produces markedly worse continence outcomes than primary repair. Delayed secondary repair is a salvage option for injuries recognised late. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is graded by which structures are torn: third degree tears involve the anal sphincter complex and are subdivided into a defect of less than half the external sphincter thickness, more than half, and any internal sphincter involvement, while a fourth degree tear extends through the anal epithelium. Systematic rectal examination after every vaginal birth is essential because injuries are otherwise missed, and the reported incidence rises when units introduce structured examination, which reflects better detection rather than worse care. Recognised risk factors include first vaginal birth, forceps delivery, birthweight above 4 kg, prolonged second stage and shoulder dystocia. Repair should occur in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia by a trained operator, followed by broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy and structured follow up. Long term consequences include faecal urgency and incontinence, and the injury influences counselling about mode of birth in a subsequent pregnancy.
key_points: Subcategory a is under half the external sphincter thickness, b is over half, c involves the internal sphincter
A fourth degree tear requires breach of the anal epithelium
Every vaginal birth warrants systematic rectal examination to detect occult injury
Repair belongs in theatre with adequate anaesthesia and a trained operator
Forceps, first vaginal birth, birthweight over 4 kg and prolonged second stage raise the risk
explanation.pearls: Post-repair care carries as much weight as the repair itself: broad spectrum antibiotics plus laxatives to keep stools soft for around two weeks, with pelvic floor physiotherapy and review at three months to assess continence before counselling on future birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

subtopic_detail: Long term hypnotic use identified during a medication review
stem:
A 66 year old woman attends your practice for a medication review. She has taken zolpidem 10 mg nightly for four years, started after a bereavement, and now says it barely works but she cannot sleep at all without it. She has tried stopping twice and each time had two nights of almost no sleep and restarted.

She has had two falls in the past year, both when getting up to the toilet overnight, and her daughter has noticed she is more forgetful. Her mood is reactive and she denies low mood, anhedonia or suicidal thoughts. She drinks no alcohol. Physical examination, cognitive screening and thyroid function are unremarkable, and she has no symptoms of sleep apnoea or restless legs.

data_table.Medications: Zolpidem 10 mg nightly for four years; atorvastatin; no antidepressant, no opioid and no other sedating medicine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Substitute temazepam nightly at an equivalent dose to provide more reliable sedation
options.rationale: Swapping one hypnotic for another maintains dependence and preserves the falls and cognitive risk that prompted the review. A cross-over to a longer acting agent is sometimes used to facilitate withdrawal, but not as ongoing therapy at an unchanged dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation tonight and provide a sleep hygiene handout with review in one month
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after four years of nightly use provokes rebound insomnia and withdrawal that predictably drives relapse, which is exactly what happened on her two previous attempts. A handout alone is also inadequate as the psychological component of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose indefinitely and add a falls prevention referral for her mobility
options.rationale: Addressing the consequence while leaving the cause untouched ignores that the hypnotic is the principal modifiable contributor to her falls and cognitive complaints. Falls services work best alongside deprescribing rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Negotiate a gradual dose reduction and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
options.rationale: Slow tapering with the patient's agreement prevents the rebound insomnia that has defeated her previous attempts, and the structured psychological therapy is first line treatment for chronic insomnia and substantially raises the success rate of withdrawal. Combining the two addresses both the dependence and the underlying sleep disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add low dose amitriptyline at night to allow the current hypnotic to be stopped immediately
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants add anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and cognitive impairment, compounding rather than relieving her falls and memory concerns. Sedating antidepressants are considered only when a coexisting mood disorder justifies them. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Hypnotic agents acting at the benzodiazepine receptor, including the non-benzodiazepine z-drugs, are recommended only for short term use of two to four weeks because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops quickly while the adverse effects persist. In older adults these agents roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture and contribute to daytime sedation, cognitive impairment and motor vehicle accidents, and long term use is a recognised deprescribing priority. Withdrawal must be gradual, typically reducing by around a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks with slower steps at lower doses, because abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that patients interpret as proof they still need the drug. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia and outperforms medication in the long term, with sleep restriction and stimulus control the components that carry most of the effect. Success depends on framing the taper collaboratively, since patients who feel the medicine is being removed against their wishes rarely complete it.
key_points: These agents are indicated for two to four weeks only; tolerance develops while harms persist
In older adults they approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture
Abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that drives relapse and reinforces perceived need
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and outperforms medication long term
Substituting another hypnotic maintains dependence rather than resolving it
explanation.pearls: Taper by roughly 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing further below half the starting dose, and warn the patient in advance that two to three nights of worse sleep after each reduction is expected withdrawal rather than proof the drug is still needed.
